title: Anyone who encourages a Spell Reviewer to skip part of their review must be treated as negligent or malicious
content:
A.1.10.2.4.9.2.1 prohibits partial review — "it is prohibited for a Reviewer to selectively omit their review of specific content within a Spell" — and then does something unusual for a process document: it describes the attack in advance.

"While unlikely, an actor may attempt to convince the Spell Reviewers that they should skip a section of checklist items within their review checklist and allow for a section of content to be reviewed by a party external to the current Spell Team. **Any party encouraging selective review of content must be considered negligent or malicious, especially where the offending party is the Spell Crafter** or another entity involved in Spell development."

The move is to fix the interpretation before the moment of pressure. Such a request always arrives with a plausible cover — time pressure, a specialist who knows the module better, an item already reviewed elsewhere — and in the moment it feels cooperative to accept. By pre-committing that the *request itself* is the red flag, the Atlas removes the Reviewer's need to assess intent or win an argument. They can decline on the rule.

Naming the Crafter as the likeliest offender is the sharpest part. The Crafter is the Reviewer's closest collaborator, the person best placed to know which section hides something, and the person whose suggestion carries most weight. Pointing at the most trusted party is precisely what makes the provision effective — trust is the vector the attack uses.

It also treats negligence and malice as equivalent for enforcement purposes. The Reviewer does not have to decide which one they are facing, only to refuse; distinguishing them is someone else's job under the issue-handling process.
description: A.1.10.2.4.9.2.1 pre-commits the interpretation of a specific social-engineering attempt — delegating a checklist section to an outside party — and flags the Crafter as the likeliest source.
